note: AI-authored, source-grounded MCQs for the official-statistics curriculum's national accounts, price, labour, agricultural, and industrial statistics competencies (batch 3), citing MoSPI/CSO/NSO manuals and metadata documents.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 2, para 2.3-2.4
questions.source_excerpt: ...the value of production, income flows and final expenditure will be identical. The significance of each arises from the fact that they reflect total operations of the economy...
questions.question: India's Gross Domestic Product can be estimated by three broad approaches that, in principle, arrive at the same total. Which set correctly names these three approaches?
options: Production approach, income approach, and expenditure approach
Census approach, sample approach, and administrative approach
Direct approach, indirect approach, and residual approach
Nominal approach, real approach, and chained approach
questions.explanation: National accounts theory holds that the value of production, the income generated by that production, and the expenditure on that production's output are conceptually identical, so GDP can be built up from any of the three sides: production (value added), income (factor incomes), or expenditure (final demand).

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 2, para 2.4
questions.source_excerpt: If output is valued by including tax less subsidy on production but not on products, we obtain GDP at basic price.
questions.question: Starting from GDP at factor cost, what must be added to arrive at GDP at basic prices?
options: Taxes less subsidies on production (excluding taxes/subsidies on products)
Taxes less subsidies on products only, including those on imports and exports
Consumption of fixed capital
Net factor income from abroad
questions.explanation: The manual's valuation chain moves from factor cost (no taxes/subsidies at all) to basic prices by adding taxes less subsidies on production -- as distinct from taxes/subsidies on products, which are added at the next step to reach market prices.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 2, para 2.4
questions.source_excerpt: To the basic price GDP if we add taxes less subsidies on products including those relating to import/export we get GDP at market price.
questions.question: Per the manual's valuation chain, GDP at market prices is obtained from GDP at basic prices by adding which item?
options: Taxes less subsidies on products, including those relating to imports and exports
Compensation of employees paid to non-residents
Consumption of fixed capital on public-sector assets
Net capital inflow from abroad
questions.explanation: The final step from basic prices to market prices adds taxes less subsidies on products (which include import/export-related taxes and subsidies) -- these are levied per unit of the product itself, unlike the production-level taxes/subsidies already folded in at the basic-price stage.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 2, para 2.3
questions.source_excerpt: ...is given by Net Domestic Product (NDP), which is nothing but GDP less CFC.
questions.question: How does the manual define Net Domestic Product (NDP) in relation to GDP?
options: NDP equals GDP less Consumption of Fixed Capital (CFC)
NDP equals GDP plus Consumption of Fixed Capital (CFC)
NDP equals GDP less net factor income from abroad
NDP equals GDP plus indirect taxes
questions.explanation: NDP nets out the wear-and-tear (depreciation) of fixed capital used up in production during the year -- it is GDP minus Consumption of Fixed Capital, giving a truer picture of sustainable output after replacing worn-out capital.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 2, para 2.3
questions.source_excerpt: A measure of the overall income of the economy obtained by adding net compensation of employees and property income received from the rest of the world is termed as Gross National Income (GNI).
questions.question: Per the manual, Gross National Income (GNI) is obtained by adding what to GDP?
options: Net compensation of employees and property income received from the rest of the world
Consumption of fixed capital on assets located abroad
Taxes less subsidies on products relating to imports
The statistical discrepancy between the production and expenditure approaches
questions.explanation: GNI extends the domestic (territorial) measure of GDP to a national (residency) measure by adding the net inflow of employee compensation and property income that residents earn from the rest of the world, net of similar outflows to non-residents.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 2, para 2.3
questions.source_excerpt: The term National Income is nothing but the Net National Income (NNI).
questions.question: According to the manual's definitions, what is 'National Income' equivalent to?
options: Net National Income (NNI), i.e. GNI less Consumption of Fixed Capital
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at market prices
Net Domestic Product (NDP) plus net factor income from abroad only, without any depreciation adjustment
Gross Value Added (GVA) at basic prices
questions.explanation: The manual equates 'National Income' with Net National Income (NNI) -- that is, GNI (the gross national aggregate, incorporating net factor income from abroad) after further deducting Consumption of Fixed Capital, mirroring how NDP relates to GDP at the domestic level.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 2, para 2.3
questions.source_excerpt: GNI and GDP are coterminous in a closed economy.
questions.question: Why does the manual state that GNI and GDP are 'coterminous' (identical) in a closed economy, but not in an open one?
options: Because a closed economy has no cross-border flows of factor income (compensation of employees or property income) to create a gap between the two
Because a closed economy always has a trade surplus, which automatically equalises GNI and GDP
Because taxes on products cannot be levied in a closed economy
Because in a closed economy, GDP is measured only using the expenditure approach
questions.explanation: GNI differs from GDP only by net factor income from abroad (compensation of employees and property income exchanged with non-residents). A closed economy has no such cross-border transactions by definition, so nothing separates GNI from GDP; an open economy's residents both earn income abroad and pay income to foreign residents, opening a gap between the two aggregates.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Introduction, Fourth revision of the base year
questions.source_excerpt: Fourth revision of the base year... as base year (hereafter referred to as 1993-...) ...auspices of the Inter Secretariat Working Group... the European Communities (EUROSTAT)... Development (OECD), United Nations and recommendations of 1993 SNA.
questions.question: The fourth revision of the base year of India's National Accounts Statistics, which shifted the base to 1993-94, was undertaken mainly to align India's national accounts with which international framework?
options: The 1993 System of National Accounts (1993 SNA), developed under an inter-agency working group including the UN, OECD and EUROSTAT
The IMF's Special Data Dissemination Standard (SDDS)
The World Bank's International Comparison Program (ICP)
The WTO's Harmonized System of trade classification
questions.explanation: The fourth base revision to 1993-94 was carried out to bring India's national accounting concepts and classifications in line with the 1993 System of National Accounts, an internationally coordinated standard developed with the UN, OECD, EUROSTAT and other agencies.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter on institutional sectors
questions.source_excerpt: ...institutional sectors into which the economy [is divided]... institutions serving households (NPISH) and government... record the production of goods and... distribution and redistribution of...
questions.question: Under the System of National Accounts framework used in India's national accounts, which of the following is one of the standard institutional sectors into which the economy is divided?
options: Non-Profit Institutions Serving Households (NPISH)
The organised and unorganised sectors of manufacturing
Census sector and sample sector
Rural, urban and combined sectors
questions.explanation: SNA-based institutional sector accounts split the economy into non-financial corporations, financial corporations, general government, households, Non-Profit Institutions Serving Households (NPISH), and the rest of the world -- NPISH is one of these six standard sectors, distinct from industry-based splits like organised/unorganised or survey-design categories like census/sample sector.

questions.locator: Manual on Estimation of State and District Income, Chapter 3, para 3.4-3.5
questions.source_excerpt: In the Income originating approach, the measurement corresponds to income originating to the factors of production physically located within the geographical boundaries of state... The State DESs presently compile estimates of SDP/DDP following the income originating approach, due to lack of requisite data needed for compiling these estimates by following the income accruing approach.
questions.question: Why do State Directorates of Economics and Statistics (DES) compile State/District Domestic Product using the 'income originating' approach rather than the 'income accruing' approach?
options: Because the data needed to track income accruing to residents regardless of where it was earned is not available at the state/district level, so income is instead measured where production physically occurs
Because the income accruing approach is legally prohibited under the Factories Act
Because income originating always yields a higher estimate, which states prefer for higher central devolution
Because the income accruing approach only applies to the informal sector
questions.explanation: The income originating approach attributes income to the geographic location where production physically occurs, which can be measured from establishment/activity-level data available within the state. The income accruing approach would require tracking income flows to residents regardless of where they earned it (e.g. remittances, cross-border employment) -- data State DESs generally lack -- so they default to income originating.

questions.locator: Manual on Estimation of State and District Income, Chapter 3, 'Per Capita Income'
questions.source_excerpt: Per Capita State Income is obtained by dividing the NSDP (State Income) by mid-year projected population of the state and is in contrast to the Per Capita National Income which is obtained by dividing the Net national Product (NNP) by the mid-year population of the country.
questions.question: How is Per Capita State Income calculated, per the manual?
options: By dividing Net State Domestic Product (NSDP) by the mid-year projected population of the state
By dividing Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) by the number of registered taxpayers in the state
By dividing Net National Product (NNP) by the mid-year population of the state
By dividing NSDP by the total workforce of the state
questions.explanation: Per Capita State Income = NSDP / mid-year projected state population -- the state-level analogue of Per Capita National Income, which instead divides Net National Product by the country's mid-year population.

questions.locator: Manual on Estimation of State and District Income, Chapter 3, para 3.19
questions.source_excerpt: The estimates for commodity producing sectors like agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining & quarrying, manufacturing, etc. are prepared using the production approach... In the services sectors (non-public segment) like trade, transport, hotels & restaurants etc., the estimates are prepared by income approach, specifically, by multiplying the value added per worker by the number of workers...
questions.question: For State Income compilation, the manual describes different methods for different sector types. How are estimates for a non-public services sector such as trade or hotels & restaurants typically prepared, in contrast to commodity-producing sectors like agriculture or manufacturing?
options: By the income approach -- multiplying value added per worker by the number of workers -- whereas commodity-producing sectors use the production approach of output minus material cost
By satellite imagery of business establishments, whereas commodity-producing sectors rely entirely on tax records
By identical production-approach methodology as commodity-producing sectors, with no distinction
By simply extrapolating the previous year's estimate using the wholesale price index
questions.explanation: The manual distinguishes methodology by sector type: commodity-producing sectors (agriculture, manufacturing, mining) use the production approach (value of output minus material inputs), while non-public services sectors like trade and hospitality use the income approach, estimating value added per worker and multiplying by the number of workers in that activity.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter on Saving and Capital Formation
questions.source_excerpt: ...economy savings equals capital formation during the year whereas for the open economy savings equals capital formation plus net capital inflow from abroad during the year.
questions.question: How does the savings-investment identity in India's national accounts differ between a closed economy and an open economy, per the manual?
options: In a closed economy, savings equals capital formation; in an open economy, savings equals capital formation plus net capital inflow from abroad
In a closed economy, savings always exceeds capital formation by the amount of government spending
In an open economy, capital formation is irrelevant and only net exports determine growth
There is no difference; the identity holds identically for both closed and open economies
questions.explanation: In a closed economy with no foreign transactions, domestic savings must exactly fund domestic capital formation. In an open economy, capital formation can also be financed by net capital inflows from abroad (borrowing from or investment by non-residents), so domestic savings plus net capital inflow together equal capital formation.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Consolidated Accounts of the Nation
questions.source_excerpt: Discrepancy shown in this Account, taking the GDP from the production approach as the control total, gives the measure of the overall difference between the production approach and the expenditure approach followed for estimation.
questions.question: In the Consolidated Accounts of the Nation, how is the 'statistical discrepancy' between the production and expenditure approaches to GDP defined?
options: It is the difference obtained by treating GDP from the production approach as the control total and comparing it against the GDP estimate from the expenditure approach
It is the difference between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices
It is always zero by construction, since India's accounts are fully reconciled at compilation
It is the gap between the Census Sector and Sample Sector estimates of value added
questions.explanation: Because India's GDP is independently estimated from both the production side and the expenditure side using different data sources, the two rarely match exactly in practice. The production-approach GDP is treated as the control total, and the residual gap against the expenditure-approach estimate is recorded as the statistical discrepancy.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Preface, Part V
questions.source_excerpt: Part-V provides eight chapters covering the methodology of compiling Input-output Transaction Tables; Quarterly and Advance estimates of GDP; Estimation of Rural-Urban Income and Net Factor Income.
questions.question: Besides the core methodology for GDP/GVA estimation, which of the following topics does Part V of the National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods (2012) manual also cover?
options: Input-Output Transaction Tables, Quarterly and Advance estimates of GDP, and estimation of Rural-Urban Income and Net Factor Income
The sampling design of the Annual Survey of Industries
The Consumer Price Index weighting diagram
The Periodic Labour Force Survey's rotational panel design
questions.explanation: Part V of the manual is dedicated to related national-accounts topics beyond the headline GDP/GVA compilation: Input-Output Transaction Tables, Quarterly and Advance GDP estimates, and the estimation of Rural-Urban Income and Net Factor Income -- ASI sampling, CPI weighting, and PLFS design belong to separate MoSPI documents entirely.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q4
questions.source_excerpt: What is the Base Year of new CPI series? Ans: The base year of the new CPI series is 2024=100.
questions.question: What is the base year of the new (revised) Consumer Price Index series introduced by MoSPI?
questions.explanation: MoSPI's new CPI series takes 2024 as the index reference period, so the series is denoted 2024=100 -- superseding the earlier 2012=100 series.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q7
questions.source_excerpt: CPI 2024 series covers 1,465 rural markets and 1,395 urban markets across 434 towns. In addition, 12 online markets are covered across 12 towns having a population of more than 25 lakh.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the market coverage of the CPI 2024 series?
options: 1,465 rural markets and 1,395 urban markets across 434 towns, plus 12 online markets in towns with population above 25 lakh
Exactly 100 markets in each state capital, with no distinction between rural and urban
Only urban markets, since CPI 2024 dropped rural price collection entirely
45 urban centres only, unchanged since the 1960-base CPI series
questions.explanation: CPI 2024 substantially expanded price collection: 1,465 rural and 1,395 urban markets across 434 towns, plus a new layer of 12 online markets in the 12 largest towns (population over 25 lakh) to capture e-commerce prices -- rural coverage was not dropped, and the market count is far larger than the 45-centre historical series.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q9
questions.source_excerpt: Index reference period: It is the period for which index equals 100... Weight reference period: It is the period for on the basis of which weights are calculated... Price reference period: It is the period during which the base prices are collected.
questions.question: For the CPI 2024 series, which combination correctly matches each reference-period concept to what it actually is?
options: Index reference period = 2024 (index equals 100); weight reference period = HCES 2023-24 (basis for weights); price reference period = calendar year 2024 (when base prices are collected)
Index reference period = HCES 2023-24; weight reference period = 2024; price reference period = 2012
All three reference periods must always be the identical single month by international convention
Weight reference period and price reference period are the same concept with two different names
questions.explanation: These are three distinct concepts that can fall in different periods: the index reference period is when the index is normalised to 100 (2024); the weight reference period is the survey period whose expenditure pattern determines the weights (HCES 2023-24, a period ending just before 2024); and the price reference period is when the actual base prices used in the index were collected (calendar year 2024).

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q19
questions.source_excerpt: What is the hierarchical structure of CPI 2024 after adopting COICOP 2018? Ans: CPI 2024 has 12 Divisions, 43 Groups, 92 Classes, and 162 Sub-classes as per COICOP 2018.
questions.question: After adopting the COICOP 2018 classification framework, how is the CPI 2024 item basket hierarchically structured?
options: 12 Divisions, 43 Groups, 92 Classes, and 162 Sub-classes
6 Groups and 23 Sub-groups, unchanged from the CPI 2012 structure
4 Sectors and 100 Items, with no intermediate aggregation levels
17 Divisions matching the 17 Sustainable Development Goals
questions.explanation: CPI 2024 restructured its classification hierarchy to follow the UN Statistics Division's COICOP 2018 framework, organised into 12 Divisions, 43 Groups, 92 Classes, and 162 Sub-classes -- a finer and internationally comparable structure than the CPI 2012 series' 6 Groups/23 Sub-groups scheme.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q20
questions.source_excerpt: Which method is used for elementary index compilation in the CPI 2024 series? Ans: The Jevons index (Short index formula) is used for compiling elementary indices in the CPI 2024 series.
questions.question: The CPI 2024 series compiles its elementary (lowest-level) indices using the Jevons 'short index' formula. What does 'short index' (chain-based) mean in this context?
options: Successive short-period (e.g. month-on-month) price ratios are linked together, rather than every month's price always being compared back to one fixed distant base period
Only items with short shelf lives, like perishable food, are included in the elementary index
The index is calculated using only the first half of the price quotations collected each month
It refers to an abbreviated version of the CPI published for internal use only, distinct from the officially released index
questions.explanation: A chain (short) index recalculates and links period-to-period price relatives (e.g. this month vs last month) successively, rather than always comparing current prices to those from a single fixed base period -- this keeps the item sample fresher and reduces the effects of substitution bias over long spans, at the cost of a small risk of chain drift.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q21
questions.source_excerpt: Which method is used for higher level index compilation in the CPI 2024 series? Ans: The Young/Modified Laspeyres' index is used for compiling higher level indices in the CPI 2024 series.
questions.question: Which index formula does the CPI 2024 series use for compiling indices above the elementary level (e.g. Sub-class, Class, Group, Division)?
options: The Young/Modified Laspeyres' index
The Jevons short index, same as the elementary level
The Fisher ideal index
The Paasche index
questions.explanation: While elementary indices use the Jevons short (chain) formula, higher-level aggregation in CPI 2024 uses the Young/Modified Laspeyres' index, which applies fixed expenditure weights (updated periodically) to the elementary indices below it.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q15
questions.source_excerpt: At All-India level, the total weighted items have been increased from 299 to 358. Specifically, goods items have risen from 259 to 308, and services items from 40 to 50.
questions.question: How did the total number of weighted items in the All-India CPI basket change from the CPI 2012 series to the CPI 2024 series?
options: It increased from 299 to 358, with both goods items (259 to 308) and services items (40 to 50) rising
It decreased from 358 to 299, as several obsolete items were dropped
It stayed exactly the same at 299 items, only the weights were revised
It increased tenfold, from about 35 to 358 items
questions.explanation: The CPI 2024 item basket was widened to better capture the economy's evolving consumption pattern: total weighted items rose from 299 to 358 at the All-India level, with growth in both goods (259 to 308) and services (40 to 50) items.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q25
questions.source_excerpt: By definition, CPI should include only items on which households actually spend money. IMF's manual on CPI also suggests that social transfer in kind should not be considered in CPI compilation. In view of this, free social transfers are excluded from the CPI.
questions.question: Why does the CPI exclude free social transfers (e.g. goods or services given to households at no cost) from its compilation, per the FAQ's stated rationale?
options: Because the CPI is defined to include only items on which households actually spend money, consistent with the IMF's CPI manual guidance excluding social transfers in kind
Because free social transfers are always negligible in value and would not move the index
Because social transfers are already counted in the National Accounts and including them would double-count GDP
Because collecting price data on subsidised or free goods is technically impossible for field enumerators
questions.explanation: The CPI is a price index of household out-of-pocket expenditure. Since a free social transfer involves no household spending, including it would misrepresent what the index is meant to measure -- a position the FAQ explicitly grounds in IMF's CPI manual, not in data-collection difficulty or double-counting with GDP.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q37
questions.source_excerpt: The Linking Factor (LF) is given by: LF = [annual average (Geometric Mean) CPI of the new series for the overlapping year] / [annual average (Geometric Mean) CPI of the old series for the same overlapping year]. The linked CPI for the earlier month t is obtained as: (linked value) = (old series value at t) x LF.
questions.question: To construct a CPI 2024-equivalent back series using the annual-overlap linking method, how is the Linking Factor (LF) calculated, and how is it then applied?
options: LF = (new series' annual average CPI for the overlap year) / (old series' annual average CPI for the same overlap year); an earlier month's old-series value is then multiplied by LF to get its new-series-equivalent value
LF = (old series' annual average CPI) / (new series' annual average CPI); the new series values are divided by LF to backdate them
LF is fixed at exactly 1.0 by international convention, so old and new series values are used interchangeably
LF = the difference between the new and old series' index values in the overlap year, added to each earlier month's index
questions.explanation: The Linking Factor is a ratio (new series overlap-year average divided by old series overlap-year average) that captures the level difference between the two series arising from base-year and methodology changes. Multiplying each earlier old-series monthly value by this ratio rescales it onto the new series' footing, producing a consistent back series.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q11
questions.source_excerpt: The Consumer Price Index (Rural, urban and combined) has been started releasing by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) since January 2011 with base year 2010=100.
questions.question: Since when has MoSPI released a unified Consumer Price Index covering Rural, Urban, and Combined sectors together, and with what base year did that series begin?
options: Since January 2011, with base year 2010=100
Since January 2024, with base year 2024=100
Since 1960, with base year 1960=100
Since Independence in 1947, as India's oldest continuously published index
questions.explanation: Before 2011, India's CPI system was fragmented across separate series (Industrial Workers, Agricultural Labourers, Rural Labourers, Urban Non-Manual Employees). MoSPI began releasing a unified national-level CPI for Rural, Urban and Combined sectors together starting January 2011, on base year 2010=100.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q17
questions.source_excerpt: In the CPI 2024 series, prices are collected using a tablet-based software application via Computer Assisted Personal Interview (CAPI), replacing the traditional paper-based method.
questions.question: How does the CPI 2024 series collect field price data from markets, compared with earlier CPI series?
options: Using a tablet-based application via Computer Assisted Personal Interview (CAPI), replacing the traditional paper-based method
Exclusively through automated web-scraping of retailer websites, with no field enumerators
Using the same paper schedules used since the 1960s, unchanged
Through crowdsourced price submissions from the general public via a mobile app
questions.explanation: CPI 2024 modernised field data collection by moving field enumerators from paper schedules to a tablet-based CAPI application -- a technology upgrade, not a shift to web-scraping or public crowdsourcing, which remain distinct (and separately used) supplementary sources for specific items like airfares.

questions.locator: Frequently Asked Questions on the CPI 2024 Series, Q16
questions.source_excerpt: Which organization collects CPI price data for MoSPI? Ans: Field Operations Division of National Sample Survey (NSS), MoSPI collects monthly price data for CPI.
questions.question: Which organisational unit is responsible for collecting the monthly price data used to compile the CPI?
options: The Field Operations Division (FOD) of the National Sample Survey, MoSPI
The Central Statistics Office's National Accounts Division
State-level Directorates of Economics and Statistics acting entirely independently of MoSPI
The Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy department
questions.explanation: Monthly CPI price quotations are collected in the field by the Field Operations Division (FOD) of the National Sample Survey under MoSPI -- distinct from the National Accounts Division (which handles GDP/GVA) or the RBI (which uses CPI data for policy but does not collect it).

questions.locator: Compilation of CPI: A Technical Note, Section B, para 3
questions.source_excerpt: If an entire index is missing, it is recommended to use the next level up in aggregation as the basis for making the imputation. For example, if all prices for oranges are missing, the index for citrus fruits can be used as the basis for making the imputation. If all citrus fruits are missing, the index for fruits is used...
questions.question: Per the Inter-Secretariat Working Group on Price Statistics (ISWG-PS) guidance NSO adopted, if the price index for an entire elementary item (e.g. oranges) is missing, what should be used to impute it?
options: The next level up in the classification hierarchy (e.g. citrus fruits), moving further up (e.g. to fruits, then to fruits and vegetables) if that too is missing
The item's index from exactly one year earlier, unadjusted
An imputed value of zero, effectively dropping the item from the index
The average of all 23 CPI sub-group indices regardless of relevance
questions.explanation: The recommended imputation principle climbs the classification hierarchy one level at a time -- oranges to citrus fruits, citrus fruits to fruits, fruits to fruits-and-vegetables -- using the closest available aggregate as a proxy for the missing item's price movement, rather than an unrelated fixed value or an unadjusted historical figure.

questions.locator: Compilation of CPI: A Technical Note, Section C, para 6, Formula I
questions.source_excerpt: Imputed Sub-group Index (Food Group) = (Last Observed Index of Sub-group) x (Food Index of Current Month/Food Index of last Observed Month).
questions.question: Under NSO's COVID-19-period CPI imputation methodology, how was a missing Food Group sub-group's index imputed?
options: By multiplying the sub-group's last observed index by the ratio of the Food & Beverages Group Index (current month to last observed month)
By multiplying the sub-group's last observed index by the ratio of the General CPI (current month to last observed month)
By carrying the previous year's index forward unchanged
By taking the simple average of all other Food Group sub-group indices
questions.explanation: Formula I applies specifically to sub-groups within the Food Group: the last observed sub-group index is scaled by the change in the Food & Beverages Group Index over the same period -- Formula II, used for Non-Food sub-groups, instead scales by the General CPI's movement, since a food item's price trend is better proxied by other food prices than by the broader economy-wide index.

questions.locator: Compilation of CPI: A Technical Note, Section A, para 2
questions.source_excerpt: The price of only those items were included which have been reported from at least 25% of markets, separately for Rural & Urban sector and constituted more than 70% weight of the respective Sub-groups/Groups.
questions.question: During the April-May 2020 CPI data-gap episode, what 'adequacy' criteria did NSO require before including a price-collected item's index at all (rather than treating it as entirely missing)?
options: The item's price had to be reported from at least 25% of markets (separately for rural and urban) and account for more than 70% of the weight of its Sub-group/Group
The item had to be reported from 100% of markets with no exceptions
The item just needed a single price quotation from anywhere in the country
The item had to be a food item, since only food prices were collected during the lockdown
questions.explanation: NSO set a dual adequacy threshold combining coverage breadth (price reported from at least 25% of markets, checked separately for rural and urban) and weight coverage (more than 70% of the relevant sub-group's/group's expenditure weight) before treating a group or sub-group's index as reliably computable rather than requiring imputation.

questions.locator: Manual on Consumer Price Index, 2010, Introduction
questions.source_excerpt: ...encompasses wholesale prices and retail prices for industrial workers, urban non-manual employees and rural labourers including agricultural labourers... CPI for Industrial Workers (IW), CPI for Agricultural Labourers (AL), CPI for Rural Labourers (RL), and CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees...
questions.question: Before the unified national CPI (Rural/Urban/Combined) began in 2011, India compiled several separate population-group-specific CPI series. Which of the following was one of them?
options: CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW)
CPI for Government Employees
CPI for Registered Companies
CPI for Foreign Nationals
questions.explanation: Historically, India compiled distinct CPI series targeted at specific population groups -- Industrial Workers (IW), Agricultural Labourers (AL), Rural Labourers (RL), and Urban Non-Manual Employees (UNME) -- each with its own base year and weighting diagram, before the unified all-population Rural/Urban/Combined CPI series was introduced in 2011.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Explanatory Note, para 1
questions.source_excerpt: The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) was designed with two major objectives... The first was to measure the dynamics in labour force participation and employment status in the short time interval of three months for only the urban areas in the Current Weekly Status (CWS). Secondly, for both rural and urban areas, to measure the labour force estimates on key parameters in both usual status (ps+ss) and CWS.
questions.question: What were the two major design objectives of the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), per its own Annual Report?
options: To track short-term (three-monthly) urban labour market dynamics via Current Weekly Status (CWS), and to provide both usual status (ps+ss) and CWS estimates for rural and urban areas alike
To replace the Population Census entirely and to conduct only a one-time employment survey
To measure only informal-sector wages, with no coverage of the formal/organised sector
To survey exclusively agricultural households, since PLFS was designed as a farm-income survey
questions.explanation: PLFS was designed to fill a gap the earlier quinquennial NSSO surveys could not: short-interval (quarterly) urban labour market tracking via CWS, on top of providing the traditional usual-status (ps+ss) and CWS estimates for both rural and urban India annually -- it is a general employment/unemployment survey, not limited to agriculture, wages, or a census replacement.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Annex, Data Collection para 1(a)
questions.source_excerpt: NSSO collected information on different aspects of labour force in its Quinquennial Surveys using paper schedules. In the PLFS information in the Schedule (Schedule 10.4) was collected from all members of the sample households using Computer-assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) method with inbuilt validation rules through Tablet.
questions.question: How did PLFS's data-collection method differ from the earlier quinquennial Employment-Unemployment surveys conducted by NSSO?
options: PLFS used Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) on tablets with inbuilt validation rules, whereas the quinquennial surveys used paper schedules
PLFS collected data only through telephonic interviews, while quinquennial surveys used door-to-door paper schedules
PLFS surveyed only household heads, while quinquennial surveys interviewed all household members
There was no methodological difference; PLFS simply renamed the same paper-based quinquennial survey
questions.explanation: PLFS moved from the traditional paper Schedule used in NSSO's quinquennial Employment-Unemployment rounds to a tablet-based CAPI method (Schedule 10.4) with inbuilt validation rules, which also allowed most data validation to happen at the time of interview rather than after data entry.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Annex, Sampling Design para 2(a)
questions.source_excerpt: Frame for PLFS (2017-18): The list of latest available Urban Frame Survey (UFS) blocks was the sampling frame for urban areas... List of 2011 Population Census villages (Panchayat wards for Kerala) constituted the rural sampling frame.
questions.question: What formed the First Stage Unit (FSU) sampling frame for PLFS 2017-18 in urban and rural areas respectively?
options: Urban Frame Survey (UFS) blocks for urban areas, and 2011 Population Census villages (Panchayat wards for Kerala) for rural areas
Voter ID lists for both urban and rural areas
Ration card registers maintained by the Department of Food and Public Distribution
GST-registered business addresses for urban areas and land revenue records for rural areas
questions.explanation: Like other NSS-family surveys, PLFS used Urban Frame Survey (UFS) blocks as the urban First Stage Unit frame, and 2011 Population Census villages (Panchayat wards in Kerala, which lacks revenue villages in the usual sense) as the rural frame -- not administrative records like voter lists, ration cards, or GST registrations.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Annex, Sampling Design para 2(d)
questions.source_excerpt: A rotational panel sampling design has been used in urban areas. In this rotational panel scheme, each selected household in urban areas is visited four times... For rural areas, in each quarter, only 25% FSUs of annual allocation... were covered so that independent estimates can be generated for each quarter. There was no revisit for the rural samples.
questions.question: How does PLFS's sample design differ between urban and rural areas to generate quarterly estimates?
options: Urban areas use a rotational panel where the same household is revisited four times over the year; rural areas instead cover a fresh 25% of the annual FSU allocation each quarter, with no household revisited
Both urban and rural areas use an identical rotational panel with four revisits per household
Rural areas use a rotational panel with revisits, while urban areas are surveyed only once a year with no quarterly breakdown
Quarterly estimates are not possible for either sector under the PLFS design
questions.explanation: The two sectors achieve quarter-wise estimation differently: urban areas track the same panel of households across four visits (one first visit plus three revisits) in a given year, enabling genuine short-term dynamics tracking, while rural areas simply rotate through a fresh quarter of the annual FSU allocation with no repeat visits, giving independent (not panel) quarterly estimates.

questions.locator: Compliance of Metadata of Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), Frequency of dissemination
questions.source_excerpt: 3.5 Frequency of dissemination: (i) Annual Report (ii) Quarterly Bulletin for urban areas
questions.question: Why does MoSPI publish a Quarterly Bulletin of PLFS labour indicators for urban areas only, and not for rural areas?
options: Because only the urban sample follows a rotational panel design that revisits the same households across the year, letting MoSPI compute genuinely quarter-wise Current Weekly Status estimates; the rural sample has no revisit, so only annual estimates are meaningful
Because rural areas are excluded from PLFS's statistical population entirely
Because urban unemployment is defined differently from rural unemployment, making rural data incomparable across quarters
Because the Quarterly Bulletin only reports Usual Status estimates, which are inherently urban-only concepts
questions.explanation: The urban rotational panel (four visits per household across the year) is specifically designed to support short-interval, quarter-wise Current Weekly Status tracking. Since rural households are surveyed only once with no revisit, rural PLFS data supports only annual (not quarterly) estimates -- rural areas are very much covered by PLFS, and both Usual Status and CWS concepts apply to both sectors.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Concepts and Definitions
questions.source_excerpt: ...on the usual status (ps+ss) approach and current weekly status approach adopted in the survey for classification of the population by activity statuses. The reference period for usual status (ps+ss) approach is 1 year and for current weekly status approach, it is 1 week.
questions.question: What is the reference period used for classifying a person's activity status under the Usual Status (ps+ss) approach, versus under the Current Weekly Status (CWS) approach?
options: Usual Status (ps+ss) uses a 1-year reference period, while Current Weekly Status uses a 1-week reference period
Both approaches use the same 1-week reference period
Usual Status uses 1 week and Current Weekly Status uses 1 year -- the reverse of the actual PLFS design
Usual Status uses 1 month and Current Weekly Status uses 1 day
questions.explanation: Usual Status (principal + subsidiary status) classifies a person based on their predominant activity over the preceding year, capturing longer-run/seasonal patterns, while Current Weekly Status classifies activity based on the 7 days preceding the survey date, capturing short-term fluctuations.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Concepts and Definitions, para 2.10.1
questions.source_excerpt: Unique identification under any one of the three broad activity statuses... was done by adopting either the major time criterion or priority criterion. The former was used for classification of persons according to the usual status approach and the latter for classification of persons according to the current status approach.
questions.question: When a person's activities during the reference period could fit more than one of the three broad activity statuses, which criterion did PLFS use to assign a single status under the Usual Status approach, versus under the CWS/CDS (current status) approaches?
options: The major time criterion for Usual Status, and the priority criterion for the current status (CWS/CDS) approaches
The priority criterion for Usual Status, and the major time criterion for the current status approaches
Both approaches use only the priority criterion; the major time criterion is not part of PLFS methodology
Both approaches use only the major time criterion; the priority criterion is not part of PLFS methodology
questions.explanation: PLFS resolves ambiguous cases differently by approach: the Usual Status approach assigns the status corresponding to the activity on which the person spent the most (major) time during the reference year, while the current status approaches (CWS and CDS) instead apply a priority ranking among the possible statuses -- both criteria are genuinely part of the methodology, just applied to different approaches.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Concepts and Definitions, para 2.10
questions.source_excerpt: A person could be in one or a combination of the following three broad activity statuses during the reference period: (i) working or being engaged in economic activity (work), (ii) being not engaged in economic activity (work) but either making tangible efforts to seek 'work' or being available for 'work'... and (iii) being not engaged in any economic activity (work) and also not available for 'work'.
questions.question: PLFS classifies every individual into one of three broad activity statuses during the reference period. What are they?
options: Engaged in economic activity (working); not engaged but seeking/available for work (unemployed); neither engaged nor available for work (not in the labour force)
Formal sector worker; informal sector worker; unpaid family worker
Rural worker; urban worker; migrant worker
Employed in agriculture; employed in industry; employed in services
questions.explanation: The three broad activity statuses map directly onto the employed / unemployed / not-in-labour-force split: engaged in economic activity is 'employed', not engaged but seeking or available for work is 'unemployed' (both counted in the labour force), and neither engaged nor available for work means being outside the labour force altogether -- distinct from sector-of-employment or formal/informal classifications, which are separate concepts.

questions.locator: Compliance of Metadata of Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), Statistical concepts and definitions
questions.source_excerpt: 1. Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR): (no. of employed persons + no. of unemployed persons) * 100 / total population
questions.question: Per MoSPI's PLFS metadata documentation, how is the Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) calculated?
options: (Number of employed persons + number of unemployed persons) / total population, expressed as a percentage
Number of employed persons / number of unemployed persons, expressed as a percentage
Number of unemployed persons / total population, expressed as a percentage
Number of employed persons / total working-age population only, excluding children and the elderly entirely from the denominator
questions.explanation: LFPR measures what share of the total population is 'in the labour force' -- i.e. either working or seeking/available for work -- so its numerator sums employed and unemployed persons (both are 'in the labour force'), divided by total population and multiplied by 100.

questions.locator: Compliance of Metadata of Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), Statistical concepts and definitions
questions.source_excerpt: 2. Worker Population Ratio (WPR): no. of employed persons * 100 / total population
questions.question: Per MoSPI's PLFS metadata documentation, how is the Worker Population Ratio (WPR) calculated?
options: Number of employed persons / total population, expressed as a percentage
Number of employed persons / number of persons in the labour force, expressed as a percentage
Number of employed persons / number of unemployed persons, expressed as a percentage
Number of employed persons in agriculture / total employed persons, expressed as a percentage
questions.explanation: WPR measures what share of the entire population is actually working, so it divides the number of employed persons directly by total population (not by the labour force, which is the denominator used for the Unemployment Rate instead) and expresses the result as a percentage.

questions.locator: Compliance of Metadata of Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), Statistical concepts and definitions
questions.source_excerpt: 3. Unemployment Rate (UR): no. of unemployed persons / (no. of employed persons + no. of unemployed persons)
questions.question: Per MoSPI's PLFS metadata documentation, the Unemployment Rate (UR) is the number of unemployed persons divided by which denominator?
options: The sum of employed and unemployed persons (i.e. the total labour force)
The total population, including those not in the labour force
The number of employed persons only
The working-age population minus the number of employed persons
questions.explanation: Unlike LFPR and WPR (which both divide by total population), the Unemployment Rate's denominator is the labour force itself -- the sum of employed and unemployed persons -- so UR answers 'of those who are working or seeking work, what fraction are without work', not 'of everyone, what fraction is unemployed'.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Section C.1
questions.source_excerpt: The Worker Population Ratio (WPR) in usual status (ps+ss) was about 34.7 per cent at the all-India level...
questions.question: According to PLFS 2017-18's own reported results, approximately what was the all-India Worker Population Ratio (WPR) in usual status (ps+ss)?
options: About 34.7 per cent
About 74.7 per cent
About 4.7 per cent
About 94.7 per cent
questions.explanation: PLFS 2017-18 reported an all-India WPR (usual status, ps+ss) of about 34.7 per cent -- meaning roughly one in three people in the total population (across all ages) were classified as workers, a figure depressed by the inclusion of children, students, and the elderly in the population base.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Section C.2
questions.source_excerpt: Share of self-employed among workers in usual status (ps+ss) was about 57.8 per cent...
questions.question: According to PLFS 2017-18, what was the approximate share of self-employed persons among all workers classified in usual status (ps+ss)?
options: About 57.8 per cent
About 15 per cent
About 90 per cent
About 5.8 per cent
questions.explanation: PLFS 2017-18 found self-employment to be the dominant employment status category, accounting for about 57.8 per cent of all usual-status (ps+ss) workers, with the remainder split between regular wage/salaried employment and casual labour.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Concepts and Definitions, para on employment status codes
questions.source_excerpt: ...self-employed (relevant activity status codes: 11, 12, 21, 61, 62), regular wage/salaried employee (relevant activity status codes: 31, 71, 72), and casual labour (relevant activity status codes: 41, 42 and 51).
questions.question: PLFS classifies every worker into one of three employment-status categories using detailed activity status codes. Which grouping of codes is correctly matched to its category?
options: Self-employed: codes 11, 12, 21, 61, 62; Regular wage/salaried: codes 31, 71, 72; Casual labour: codes 41, 42, 51
Self-employed: codes 41, 42, 51; Regular wage/salaried: codes 11, 12, 21; Casual labour: codes 31, 71, 72
All three categories share the exact same set of codes, distinguished only by industry
Self-employed: codes 31, 71, 72; Regular wage/salaried: codes 41, 42, 51; Casual labour: codes 11, 12, 21, 61, 62
questions.explanation: PLFS's detailed activity-status coding scheme assigns a distinct block of codes to each employment-status category: 11/12/21/61/62 for self-employed (own-account workers, employers, unpaid family workers), 31/71/72 for regular wage/salaried employees, and 41/42/51 for casual labour -- these blocks do not overlap.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Section C.5
questions.source_excerpt: 68.4 per cent of the workers in usual status (ps+ss) in non-agriculture and...[were in the informal sector]
questions.question: According to PLFS 2017-18, roughly what proportion of usual-status (ps+ss) workers in the non-agriculture sector were engaged in the informal sector?
options: About 68.4 per cent
About 10 per cent
About 99 per cent
About 33 per cent
questions.explanation: PLFS 2017-18 found that informality remained pervasive outside agriculture: about 68.4 per cent of non-agricultural usual-status (ps+ss) workers were in the informal sector, underscoring the limited reach of formal-sector employment relative to India's overall workforce.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Annex, Stratification para 3(a)
questions.source_excerpt: Stratification for first stage units in PLFS: In urban areas strata were formed within each NSS region on the basis of size class of towns as per Population Census 2011. stratum 1: all towns with population less than 50,000; stratum 2: 50,000 or more but less than 3 lakhs; stratum 3: 3 lakhs or more but less than 15 lakhs; stratum 4,5,6...: each city with population 15 lakhs or more.
questions.question: How did PLFS stratify urban First Stage Units (towns) within each NSS region for sampling purposes?
options: By town population size class as per Census 2011 -- towns under 50,000; 50,000 to under 3 lakh; 3 lakh to under 15 lakh; and each city of 15 lakh or more forming its own separate stratum
By the town's per-capita income, ranked into deciles
Alphabetically by town name, divided into equal-sized groups
By whether the town had an operational Annual Survey of Industries unit
questions.explanation: PLFS used a population-size-based stratification of towns drawn from Census 2011 figures, with the very largest cities (15 lakh population and above) each forming their own individual stratum -- a design choice that ensures large, heterogeneous metros are not lumped together with smaller towns of similar size class.

questions.locator: Annual Report, PLFS 2017-18, Annex, Sampling Design para 2(a)-2(b)
questions.source_excerpt: Frame for PLFS (2017-18): ...For nearly one-half of the towns, UFS frame 2012-17 was used and for another half of the towns, UFS frame 2007-12 was used. List of 2011 Population Census villages... constituted the rural sampling frame. Frame for 68th round (2011-12): The first stage units (FSU) were the 2001 census villages... For NSS 68th round (2011-12), UFS frame 2007-12 was used.
questions.question: How did the sampling frame vintage used in PLFS (2017-18) differ from that used in the NSS 68th round Employment-Unemployment Survey (2011-12)?
options: PLFS used the newer 2011 Census villages and a mix of UFS frames from 2012-17 and 2007-12, whereas the 68th round used 2001 Census villages and only the 2007-12 UFS frame
Both surveys used identical sampling frames with no changes whatsoever
PLFS used the older 2001 Census villages, while the 68th round used the newer 2011 Census villages
Neither survey used a UFS frame; both relied solely on revenue village lists
questions.explanation: As successive rounds of Census and Urban Frame Survey data become available, NSS-family surveys update their sampling frames -- PLFS 2017-18 moved to 2011 Census villages and blended UFS frames from two update cycles (2012-17 for about half the towns, 2007-12 for the rest), a more current frame than the 68th round's 2001 Census villages and single 2007-12 UFS frame.

questions.locator: Compliance of Metadata of Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), Statistical unit and population coverage
questions.source_excerpt: PLFS covers the whole of the Indian Union except the villages in Andaman and Nicobar Islands which are difficult to access.
questions.question: What is the one notable geographic exclusion from PLFS's otherwise nationwide population coverage?
options: Villages in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands that are difficult to access
All of North-Eastern India
All Union Territories without a legislature
Metropolitan cities with a population above one crore
questions.explanation: PLFS otherwise covers the whole of the Indian Union, but explicitly excludes villages in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands that are difficult to access -- a narrow, logistics-driven exclusion, not a broader regional or city-size-based one.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.1.1 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: Indicator 2.1.1: Percentage of children aged under 5 years who are underweight. Data Source Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Data is collected in NFHS. Numerator: Children aged 0-59 months who are underweight; Denominator: Number of children in age group 0-59 months.
questions.question: Per the SDG National Indicator Framework's Indicator 2.1.1, which ministry is the data source for the percentage of children under 5 years who are underweight, and through which survey is the underlying data collected?
options: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, with data collected through the National Family Health Survey (NFHS)
Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare, with data collected through the Agriculture Census
Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, with data collected through the Annual Survey of Industries
Ministry of Rural Development, with data collected through the Socio-Economic Caste Census
questions.explanation: Indicator 2.1.1 (underweight children under 5) is a health/nutrition indicator: its data source ministry is Health and Family Welfare, and the underlying data comes from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS) -- not an agriculture-sector ministry or survey, even though the indicator sits under SDG Goal 2's food-security and nutrition theme.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.1.2 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: Indicator 2.1.2: Proportion of beneficiaries covered under National Food Security Act 2013. Data Source Ministry: Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. Numerator: Families/persons identified under NFSA; Denominator: Accepted number of persons covered under NFSA.
questions.question: Indicator 2.1.2 of the SDG National Indicator Framework tracks the proportion of beneficiaries covered under a specific piece of legislation. Which one, and which ministry is its data source?
options: The National Food Security Act, 2013, with the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution as the data source
The Right to Education Act, with the Ministry of Education as the data source
The Minimum Wages Act, with the Ministry of Labour and Employment as the data source
The Essential Commodities Act, with the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare as the data source
questions.explanation: Indicator 2.1.2 measures coverage under the National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013 -- families/persons identified under NFSA as a proportion of the accepted number covered -- and its data source ministry is Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, which administers the public distribution system underlying NFSA.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.2.1 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.2.1: Percentage of children under age 5 years who are stunted... defined as percentage of children aged 0-59 months who are stunted (short for age i.e. children whose height-for-age is below minus 2 times standard deviation from the WHO Child Growth Standards median).
questions.question: How does the SDG National Indicator Framework define a child as 'stunted' under Indicator 2.2.1?
options: A child aged 0-59 months whose height-for-age is below minus 2 standard deviations from the WHO Child Growth Standards median
A child aged 0-59 months whose weight-for-height is below minus 2 standard deviations from the WHO Child Growth Standards median
A child aged 0-59 months who has not received any vaccination
A child aged 0-59 months whose Body Mass Index exceeds the 95th percentile
questions.explanation: Stunting is specifically a height-for-age deficit (chronic malnutrition, 'short for age'), defined as height-for-age below minus 2 SD of the WHO Child Growth Standards median -- this is distinct from wasting, which the framework separately defines using weight-for-height.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.2.2 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.2.2: Prevalence of malnutrition among children under 5 years of age, by type (wasting and overweight)... percentage of Children aged 0-59 months who are wasted (weight-for-height is below minus 2 standard deviation...) and overweight (weight-for-height is above 2 standard deviation...).
questions.question: Indicator 2.2.2 tracks both 'wasting' and 'overweight' among children under 5 using the same underlying measurement (weight-for-height). How does the framework distinguish the two conditions?
options: Wasting is weight-for-height below minus 2 standard deviations of the WHO median; overweight is weight-for-height above plus 2 standard deviations of the WHO median
Wasting is measured in rural areas only, and overweight is measured in urban areas only
Wasting refers to children under 2 years, and overweight refers to children aged 2-5 years
There is no distinction; 'wasting and overweight' is treated as a single combined category
questions.explanation: Both conditions are anchored to the same weight-for-height distribution relative to the WHO Child Growth Standards median, but at opposite tails: wasting is an acute deficit (below minus 2 SD, indicating recent/severe malnutrition), while overweight is an excess (above plus 2 SD) -- neither is defined by geography or a specific narrow age band within the 0-59 month range.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.2.3 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.2.3 Prevalence of anaemia in women aged 15 to 49 years, by pregnancy status (percentage)... percentage of pregnant, non-pregnant and total women aged 15-49 years who are anaemic. Data is collected under NFHS.
questions.question: Indicator 2.2.3's anaemia prevalence figures for women aged 15-49 are disaggregated by which factor, per the framework's own description?
options: Pregnancy status (pregnant, non-pregnant, and total)
Educational attainment level only
Household landholding size
Type of employment (agricultural vs non-agricultural)
questions.explanation: Indicator 2.2.3 is explicitly computed separately for pregnant women, non-pregnant women, and the total of both groups aged 15-49, since anaemia risk and its public-health implications differ substantially by pregnancy status; it is not disaggregated by education, landholding, or employment type in its own definition.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.2.4 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.2.4: Percentage of women whose Body Mass Index (BMI) is below normal... Numerator: Number of women aged 15-49 years with BMI <18.5kg/sq. meter; Denominator: Total number of women aged 15-49 years whose height and weight are measured.
questions.question: Per Indicator 2.2.4, what BMI threshold defines a woman aged 15-49 as having 'below normal' BMI?
options: BMI below 18.5 kg per square metre
BMI below 25 kg per square metre
BMI above 30 kg per square metre
BMI exactly equal to 20 kg per square metre
questions.explanation: The indicator's own numerator definition sets the below-normal (underweight) threshold at a BMI under 18.5 kg/sq. metre -- the standard clinical cutoff for adult underweight status, distinct from the (higher) thresholds used to define overweight or obesity.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.3.2 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.3.2: Gross Value Added in Agriculture per worker... Numerator: GVA in Agriculture and Allied sectors (at constant price); Denominator: Total number of agricultural workers. Unit: Rs. Per Worker.
questions.question: How is Indicator 2.3.2, 'Gross Value Added in Agriculture per worker', computed?
options: Gross Value Added in Agriculture and Allied sectors at constant prices, divided by the total number of agricultural workers
Total agricultural output value divided by the total cultivated area in hectares
Total government subsidy to agriculture divided by the number of registered farmers
Gross Value Added in Agriculture at current prices, divided by the total rural population
questions.explanation: The indicator is a labour-productivity measure for agriculture: GVA in Agriculture and Allied sectors valued at constant prices (to strip out pure price effects) divided by the number of agricultural workers, giving output per worker in rupees -- not a land-productivity, subsidy-intensity, or population-based ratio.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.3.3 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.3.3: Ratio of institutional Credit to Agriculture to the Agriculture output... The indicator which is the ratio of Agri Credit to Agriculture Gross Value Output (GVO), indicates the intensity of credit in agriculture. Higher the level of development, higher the intensity expected.
questions.question: What does Indicator 2.3.3, the ratio of institutional credit to agriculture output, actually measure, per the framework's own description?
options: The intensity of institutional credit flowing into agriculture relative to agricultural output, where a higher ratio is associated with a higher level of agricultural development
The default rate on agricultural loans issued by nationalised banks
The total number of farmers who have ever taken an agricultural loan
The interest rate charged on short-term crop loans compared to long-term agricultural term loans
questions.explanation: The indicator is explicitly framed as a measure of credit intensity in agriculture (institutional credit relative to Agriculture Gross Value Output), which the framework states is expected to rise with the level of agricultural development -- it is not a default-rate, headcount, or interest-rate-comparison measure.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.4.2 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.4.2: Percentage of farmers issued Soil Health Card... Soil Health Card is field specific detailed report of soil fertility and other important soil parameters that affect crop productivity, besides an advisory on soil test based use of fertilizers and amendments.
questions.question: What is a 'Soil Health Card', as described in the SDG National Indicator Framework's metadata for Indicator 2.4.2?
options: A field-specific report of soil fertility and other soil parameters affecting crop productivity, including an advisory on soil-test-based fertilizer and amendment use
A digital identity card issued to farmers for accessing Minimum Support Price procurement centres
A certificate proving a farmer's land is free of pest infestation
A loan eligibility document issued by cooperative banks based on landholding size
questions.explanation: The Soil Health Card is a soil-testing report tied to a specific field, documenting fertility parameters and giving fertilizer/amendment advisories based on those test results -- it is not an identity document, a pest-free certificate, or a bank loan-eligibility instrument.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.4.3 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.4.3: Percentage of net area under organic farming... National Program for Organic Production (NPOP) provides policies for development and certification of organic products... Numerator: Area under organic farming (as registered under National Programme for Organic Production certification process); Denominator: Net sown area under crops.
questions.question: How is Indicator 2.4.3, 'percentage of net area under organic farming', computed, and which programme certifies the organic area counted in the numerator?
options: Area registered under the National Programme for Organic Production (NPOP) certification process, divided by total net sown area under crops
Total number of organic farmers, divided by the total number of registered farmers nationwide
Area under organic farming divided by the area under chemical-input farming, expressed as an odds ratio
Export value of organic produce, divided by total agricultural export value
questions.explanation: The indicator's numerator is specifically the area registered under NPOP's certification process (the government's official organic-certification programme, jointly with APEDA), expressed as a share of the net sown area under crops -- not a farmer headcount, an odds ratio against conventional farming, or an export-value ratio.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.5.1 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.5.1: Number of (a) plant and (b) animal genetic resources for food and agriculture secured in either medium- or long-term conservation facilities... Plant component: Number of accessions conserved in the base collection (-18C) at National Gene bank (Seeds) + accessions Conserved In Vitro Gene bank (Tissue Cultures) + accessions at Cryogen bank (-196C). Animal component: Cryopreservation of semen at National Gene Bank + Cryopreservation of somatic cell at National Gene Bank.
questions.question: Indicator 2.5.1 counts plant and animal genetic resources secured in conservation facilities. Which of the following is one of the plant-component facilities the framework specifies?
options: The National Gene Bank's base seed collection maintained at -18 degrees Celsius
A live seed-exchange market where farmers trade seeds informally
District-level cold storage warehouses used for onion and potato stockpiling
State-run agricultural universities' teaching farms
questions.explanation: The plant component of Indicator 2.5.1 sums accessions across three formal ex-situ conservation facilities: the National Gene Bank's -18C base seed collection, an In Vitro Gene Bank for tissue cultures, and a Cryogen Bank at -196C -- informal seed markets, commodity cold storage, and teaching farms are not part of this indicator's defined scope.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.5.2 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.5.2: Proportion of local and transboundary breeds classified as being at risk of extinction... Local breeds: Annual. Transboundary breeds: Five years. Transboundary breeds: Data are available by country under DAD-IS.
questions.question: Indicator 2.5.2 tracks local and transboundary livestock breeds at risk of extinction using two different periodicities. Which is correctly matched?
options: Local breeds are assessed annually, while transboundary breeds (tracked via the international DAD-IS database) are assessed every five years
Both local and transboundary breeds are assessed on the same annual cycle
Local breeds are assessed every five years, while transboundary breeds are assessed annually
Neither component has a defined periodicity in the framework
questions.explanation: The framework specifies different periodicities for the indicator's two components: local breeds (with known risk status compiled domestically) are updated annually, whereas transboundary breeds -- which rely on the internationally maintained DAD-IS (Domestic Animal Diversity Information System) database -- are reported only every five years.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.5.3 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.5.3: Conservation of fish genetic resource (in number)... Computation: Voucher Accessions + Tissue Accessions + Accession relating to Species Wild Sourced, Propagated/Non-propagated + Fish cell lines Accessions.
questions.question: How is Indicator 2.5.3, 'Conservation of fish genetic resource', computed, per the framework's metadata?
options: As the sum of Voucher Accessions, Tissue Accessions, Accessions of wild-sourced (propagated/non-propagated) species, and Fish cell line Accessions
As the total weight (in tonnes) of fish stock held in cold storage nationwide
As the ratio of farmed fish production to total fish production
As the number of licensed inland fisheries cooperatives
questions.explanation: This indicator counts conserved fish genetic material across several accession types -- voucher accessions, tissue accessions, wild-sourced species accessions (both propagated and non-propagated), and fish cell line accessions -- summed together, rather than measuring stock tonnage, aquaculture's production share, or cooperative counts.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.a.1 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.a.1: The agriculture orientation index for government expenditures... defined as the Agriculture share of Government Expenditure, divided by the Agriculture value added share of GDP. Agriculture Share of Government Expenditures = Central Government expenditure on Agriculture / Total Central Government Expenditure * 100... Agriculture Value Added Share of GDP = Agriculture Value Added / GDP * 100.
questions.question: The Agriculture Orientation Index (AOI) for Government Expenditures, Indicator 2.a.1, is calculated as which ratio?
options: (Agriculture share of Central Government expenditure) divided by (Agriculture value-added share of GDP)
(Agriculture value-added share of GDP) divided by (Agriculture share of Central Government expenditure)
Total Central Government expenditure on Agriculture, expressed in absolute rupee terms with no ratio at all
(Agriculture exports) divided by (Total Central Government expenditure on Agriculture)
questions.explanation: The AOI compares how much government spending is oriented toward agriculture relative to how important agriculture is to the overall economy: it divides the agriculture share of Central Government expenditure by agriculture's value-added share of GDP -- an AOI of 1 would mean government spending is exactly proportionate to agriculture's economic weight.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.a.2 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.a.2: Percentage share of expenditure in Intellectual Property Product (R&D) in agriculture to GVA in agriculture... Numerator: Total Expenditure on IPP in Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing during reference year; Denominator: Gross Value Added in agriculture, Forestry and Fishing during reference year.
questions.question: Indicator 2.a.2 measures R&D intensity in agriculture. What exactly does it divide by what?
options: Total expenditure on Intellectual Property Products (R&D) in Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing, divided by the Gross Value Added of Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing
Number of patents filed by agricultural universities, divided by the number of agricultural universities
Total agricultural export earnings, divided by total agricultural R&D expenditure
Central Government expenditure on agricultural extension services, divided by the number of extension officers
questions.explanation: This indicator is an R&D-intensity ratio specific to the agriculture, forestry and fishing sector: expenditure on Intellectual Property Products (which in national accounts terms includes R&D spending) as a share of that sector's own Gross Value Added -- not a patent-count ratio, an export/R&D ratio, or an extension-staffing ratio.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Target 2.b metadata
questions.source_excerpt: Target 2.b: Correct and prevent trade restrictions and distortions in world agricultural markets, including through the parallel elimination of all forms of agricultural export subsidies... National indicator is under development.
questions.question: What does the SDG National Indicator Framework 2026 report for Target 2.b, on correcting trade restrictions and distortions in world agricultural markets (including eliminating agricultural export subsidies)?
options: That the national indicator for this target is under development, i.e. not yet finalised
That India has fully met this target with a national indicator value of zero export subsidies
That this target has been permanently dropped from India's National Indicator Framework
That this target is measured using the same indicator as Target 2.4 on sustainable food production
questions.explanation: Not every global SDG target yet has a finalised national indicator; the framework explicitly marks Target 2.b's national indicator as 'under development' rather than reporting a value, a zero, or reusing an unrelated target's indicator -- a genuine and honestly documented data gap, not a policy claim of having met the target.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicator 2.c.1 metadata
questions.source_excerpt: 2.c.1: Percentage of Agriculture Mandis enrolled in e-market... Electronic National Agriculture Market (e-NAM) is an online trading platform for agriculture commodities. Numerator: Total number of e-NAM Mandis; Denominator: Total number of Mandis.
questions.question: Indicator 2.c.1 tracks the reach of India's electronic agricultural marketing platform. How is it computed, and what is that platform called?
options: The number of Mandis enrolled in the Electronic National Agriculture Market (e-NAM) divided by the total number of Mandis
The total trading volume on e-NAM divided by the total trading volume across all physical Mandis
The number of farmers registered on e-NAM divided by the total farming population
The number of states that have passed e-NAM-enabling legislation divided by the total number of states
questions.explanation: Indicator 2.c.1 is an enrolment-coverage ratio: the count of Mandis (agricultural produce markets) enrolled in e-NAM (Electronic National Agriculture Market, an online commodity trading platform) divided by the total number of Mandis nationwide -- it measures market reach, not trading volume, farmer registration, or legislative status.

questions.locator: SDG National Indicator Framework 2026, Indicators 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.2.1-2.2.4, 2.4.2 metadata (Periodicity fields)
questions.source_excerpt: 2.1.1 Periodicity: 3 years... 2.2.1 Periodicity: 3 years... 2.2.2 Periodicity: 3 years... 2.2.3 Periodicity: 3 years... 2.2.4 Periodicity: 3 years... 2.1.2 Periodicity: Annual... 2.4.2 Periodicity: Annual.
questions.question: Comparing the periodicities documented across Goal 2's nutrition indicators (underweight, stunting, wasting/overweight, anaemia, low BMI) versus its administrative-scheme indicators (NFSA coverage, Soil Health Card issuance), what pattern emerges?
options: The nutrition indicators, all sourced from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS), share a 3-year periodicity, while the administrative-data indicators (NFSA, Soil Health Card) are reported annually
All Goal 2 indicators, regardless of data source, share the exact same monthly periodicity
The nutrition indicators are annual while the administrative-scheme indicators are only reported once a decade
Periodicity in the National Indicator Framework is unrelated to the underlying data source or survey cycle
