questions.explanation: An indicator's periodicity in the framework tracks the update cycle of its underlying data source: the nutrition indicators (2.1.1, 2.2.1-2.2.4) all draw on NFHS, a survey conducted roughly every 3 years, so they share that periodicity, while NFSA coverage and Soil Health Card issuance are drawn from continuously maintained administrative/scheme records and so are reported annually -- periodicity is very much tied to data source, not arbitrary or uniform across indicators.

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions para 15
questions.source_excerpt: Factory is one, which is registered under Sections 2m(i) and 2m(ii) of the Factories Act, 1948... (i) wherein ten or more workers are working... and a manufacturing process is being carried on with the aid of power... or (ii) wherein twenty or more workers are working... and a manufacturing process is being carried on without the aid of power...
questions.question: Under the Factories Act, 1948 definitions ASI relies on, what are the two legal thresholds under which a premises is registered as a 'factory'?
options: 10 or more workers with a manufacturing process using power [Section 2(m)(i)], OR 20 or more workers with a manufacturing process not using power [Section 2(m)(ii)]
50 or more workers using power, OR 100 or more workers not using power, with no legal minimum below that
Any premises with at least one worker, regardless of power use
100 or more workers, regardless of whether power is used
questions.explanation: The Factories Act's registration threshold is a dual, power-dependent rule: Section 2(m)(i) covers premises with 10 or more workers where a power-aided manufacturing process occurs, while Section 2(m)(ii) covers premises with 20 or more workers where the process runs without power. This is the legal definition of a 'factory' eligible for ASI's frame -- distinct from the separate census-sector/sample-sector worker thresholds used later to decide how a registered factory is sampled within ASI.

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions para 37
questions.source_excerpt: REFERENCE PERIOD: For ASI it is corresponding financial year. For example, for ASI 2005-2006 the reference period is the financial year commencing from 1st April 2005 and ending on 31st March 2006 or the accounting year of the factory ending on any date between 1.4.05 to 31.3.06.
questions.question: What is the 'reference period' for an ASI round, per the manual's own example (ASI 2005-06)?
options: The corresponding financial year -- either 1 April to 31 March, or the factory's own accounting year ending on any date within that financial year
A fixed calendar year (1 January to 31 December) for every factory regardless of its own accounting practices
A single reference date (31 March) on which a snapshot of the factory is taken
The five-year period since the previous ASI round
questions.explanation: ASI's reference period tracks the factory's own accounting year, which for most factories coincides with the financial year (April-March) but can end on any date within that window -- it is not a rigid calendar-year snapshot or a multi-year period.

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions para 17
questions.source_excerpt: Fixed Capital represents the depreciated value of fixed assets owned by the factory as on the closing day of the accounting year. Fixed assets are those, which have normal productive life of more than one year.
questions.question: How does the ASI manual define 'Fixed Capital'?
options: The depreciated value, as on the closing day of the accounting year, of assets owned by the factory that have a normal productive life of more than one year
The total wage bill paid to factory workers during the accounting year
The value of raw materials and stores held in inventory at year-end
The market capitalisation of the company that owns the factory
questions.explanation: Fixed Capital is a stock concept -- the depreciated (net) book value, at the accounting year's close, of durable assets (land, buildings, plant, machinery, transport equipment, etc.) that will be used in production over more than one year -- distinct from wages (a flow), inventory (working capital), or market capitalisation (a financial-market concept unrelated to ASI's physical-asset framework).

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions para 42
questions.source_excerpt: Working Capital is the sum total of the physical working capital as already defined above and the cash deposits in hand and at bank, land, the net balance of amounts receivable over amounts payable... It excludes unused overdraft facility, fixed deposits irrespective of duration, advances for acquisition of fixed assets, long-term loans including interest thereon and investment.
questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly excluded from ASI's definition of 'Working Capital'?
options: Fixed deposits, irrespective of duration, and long-term loans including interest
Cash deposits in hand and at bank
The net balance of amounts receivable over amounts payable
Physical working capital, such as stocks of materials and semi-finished goods
questions.explanation: ASI's Working Capital combines physical working capital with cash/bank deposits and net receivables, but deliberately excludes items that are not short-term operating liquidity: fixed deposits (regardless of tenure), unused overdraft facilities, advances for fixed-asset purchases, long-term loans and their interest, and investments -- these belong to the factory's longer-term financing structure, not its working capital.

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions para 36
questions.source_excerpt: 36. This is the total of fixed capital and working capital.
questions.question: How does the ASI manual define 'Total Capital' for a factory?
options: As the sum of Fixed Capital and Working Capital
As the sum of Gross Value of Output and Net Value Added
As the factory's total wage bill plus its total tax liability
As the difference between Fixed Capital and Working Capital
questions.explanation: 'Total Capital' in the ASI framework is simply the sum of the factory's Fixed Capital (durable productive assets) and its Working Capital (short-term operating funds) -- a straightforward addition, not a subtraction or a mix of output/wage/tax concepts from a different part of the schedule.

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Sampling Frame
questions.source_excerpt: ...frame is being revised/updated every year by the Field Operations Division of NSSO...
questions.question: Within MoSPI, which body is responsible for annually revising and updating the ASI sampling frame (the list of registered factories)?
options: The Field Operations Division of the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO)
The Reserve Bank of India's Department of Statistics
The Registrar General of India
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade
questions.explanation: While the underlying lists of registered factories originate with the Chief Inspector of Factories in each state, it is the Field Operations Division of NSSO that annually revises and updates the consolidated ASI sampling frame drawn from those state lists -- neither the RBI, the Registrar General, nor the DGFT play this role in ASI's frame maintenance.

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions para 15
questions.source_excerpt: Closed factories with fixed assets on site are also considered as registered factories till they are de-registered and removed from the live-register maintained by the Chief Inspector of Factories (CIF) in the State.
questions.question: Does a factory that has stopped operating (closed) but still has its fixed assets on site remain part of ASI's frame of registered factories?
options: Yes -- it continues to be treated as a registered factory until it is formally de-registered and removed from the Chief Inspector of Factories' live register
No -- any factory that stops production is automatically dropped from the frame the same year
Only if it resumes production within six months of closing
Only if it belongs to the public sector
questions.explanation: ASI's frame follows the formal legal registration status maintained by the state's Chief Inspector of Factories, not the factory's actual operating status -- a closed factory with fixed assets still on site remains 'registered' (and thus in-frame) until it is affirmatively de-registered, regardless of ownership sector or how quickly it might resume production.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 1, para 1.36
questions.source_excerpt: The estimates of GDP for the year 2004-05 in the new series have been compiled from the results of ASI, 2004-05. In the previous NAS series, the ASI results were used only for the year 1999-2000. For other years, the data of Index of Industrial Production (IIP) was used to extrapolate the base year estimates.
questions.question: How did the method for estimating registered manufacturing's GVA change between the old NAS series (base 1999-2000) and the new series (base 2004-05 onward)?
options: The old series used actual ASI results only for the base year (1999-2000) and extrapolated other years using the Index of Industrial Production (IIP); the new series uses actual annual ASI results directly for each year
Both series used actual annual ASI results for every year with no extrapolation at all
The old series used IIP for the base year and ASI for all subsequent years, the reverse of the new series
Registered manufacturing was not estimated at all in the old series
questions.explanation: The old series had only a single ASI-based benchmark (1999-2000), with all other years' registered-manufacturing GVA extrapolated using IIP movements -- a proxy approach. The base revision to 2004-05 allowed the new series to use actual ASI results for that year, and the manual describes the practice of using ASI results directly in compiling the annual accounts going forward, reducing reliance on IIP as a proxy.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 1, para 1.37
questions.source_excerpt: The GVA estimates for the new series for the base year 2004-05 have been prepared separately for two segments of the unregistered manufacturing, namely (i) the segment of micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) (other than those covered under the ASI), and (ii) the rest of unorganized manufacturing, i.e. the manufacturing activity which is not covered under either the ASI or the MSME.
questions.question: For national-accounts purposes, how is 'unregistered manufacturing' (activity not covered by the ASI) further split for GVA estimation?
options: Into (i) a Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) segment not covered under ASI, and (ii) a residual segment of unorganised manufacturing not covered under either ASI or the MSME segment
Into rural unregistered manufacturing and urban unregistered manufacturing only
Into export-oriented units and domestic-market units
It is not split at all; all unregistered manufacturing is estimated as a single undifferentiated block
questions.explanation: Beyond the ASI-covered 'registered' segment, the manual splits the remaining unregistered manufacturing activity into two distinct estimation segments -- the MSME segment (using MSME Census-based data) and a residual segment covering manufacturing activity outside both ASI and the MSME segment -- each estimated with its own separate data sources and methodology, not a single undifferentiated rural/urban or export/domestic split.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 1, para 1.38
questions.source_excerpt: The GVA for the MSME segment in the new series has been estimated using the value of output data available from the results of Fourth All India Census on Micro, Small and Medium enterprises, 2006-07... and the GVA/GVO ratios available from the Directory Manufacturing Enterprises (DME) (i.e. those employing 6 and above workers) results of NSS 62nd round survey on unorganized manufacturing.
questions.question: Which two data sources were combined to estimate the GVA of the MSME segment of unregistered manufacturing in the base-year (2004-05) national accounts?
options: Value-of-output data from the Fourth All India Census of MSMEs (2006-07), combined with GVA/GVO ratios from the NSS 62nd round survey of Directory Manufacturing Enterprises (6 or more workers)
Only the results of the Annual Survey of Industries, with no separate MSME-specific source
Only Income Tax Department filings by MSME-registered units
Only the decennial Population Census's economic-activity tables
questions.explanation: Since the MSME segment falls outside ASI's coverage, its GVA is instead built up from two complementary sources: output values from the periodic MSME Census (Fourth All India Census, 2006-07 for the 2004-05 base) and GVA/GVO ratios estimated from the NSS 62nd round's Directory Manufacturing Enterprises (units with 6+ workers) survey -- ASI, income tax filings, and the Population Census play no role in this specific estimation.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 1, para 1.39
questions.source_excerpt: The estimates of other unregistered manufacturing units... have been compiled using information on GVA per worker from the integrated surveys of enterprises and households excl. MSME cases in the 62nd round... The estimates of workforce for this portion... have been obtained from the total work force on manufacturing activities by subtracting the workforce relating to ASI and MSME (non-ASI) segments.
questions.question: How is the workforce figure used to estimate the residual ('other') unregistered manufacturing segment's GVA (via GVA-per-worker) actually derived?
options: By subtracting the workforce already counted under ASI and under the MSME (non-ASI) segment from the total manufacturing workforce, leaving a residual workforce for this segment
By directly surveying only this residual segment with its own dedicated census, independent of any other workforce figures
By assuming this segment's workforce equals the ASI segment's workforce, on a one-to-one basis
By using the decennial Population Census's total working-age population figure unadjusted
questions.explanation: Rather than directly surveying this residual, hard-to-enumerate segment for workforce, the manual derives its workforce as a residual: total manufacturing workforce minus the workforce already accounted for under ASI and under the MSME (non-ASI) segment -- this residual workforce is then multiplied by GVA-per-worker (from the NSS 62nd round, excluding MSME cases) to obtain the segment's GVA.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012, Chapter 1, para 1.110
questions.source_excerpt: Registered manufacturing... data of Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) in [compiling GVA/GFCF estimates].
questions.question: Which survey is the primary data source for estimating the GVA of the 'registered manufacturing' segment in India's national accounts?
options: The Annual Survey of Industries (ASI)
The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)
The Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES)
The SDG National Indicator Framework
questions.explanation: 'Registered manufacturing' is, by definition, the set of factories covered by the ASI (those meeting the Factories Act's registration thresholds), so ASI results are the natural and primary data source national accounts use to estimate this segment's GVA -- PLFS, HCES, and the SDG framework serve entirely different statistical purposes.

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions on Emoluments
questions.source_excerpt: ...in terms of gross value i.e. before deductions for fines, damages, taxes, provident fund, employees state insurance contribution etc.
questions.question: When ASI records 'emoluments' paid to factory workers, are these recorded before or after statutory deductions like provident fund, ESI contributions, taxes, and fines?
options: Before such deductions -- emoluments are recorded in gross terms
After such deductions -- only the worker's net take-home pay is recorded
Only the employer's share of provident fund is included, with the worker's own contribution excluded
Emoluments are recorded net of income tax only, but gross of all other deductions
questions.explanation: ASI records emoluments on a gross basis -- the full amount earned before fines, damages, taxes, provident fund, and ESI contributions are deducted -- because the survey is measuring the total labour cost/compensation generated by the factory's operations, not the worker's residual take-home pay.

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions para 16
questions.source_excerpt: Finished goods are those, which are manufactured by the factory for sale. Finished goods should conform to a prescribed standard.
questions.question: How does the ASI manual define 'Finished goods'?
options: Goods manufactured by the factory for sale, which conform to a prescribed standard
Any raw material purchased by the factory, regardless of processing stage
Goods that are still in the production process and not yet ready for sale
Goods manufactured by the factory exclusively for its own internal use, never for sale
questions.explanation: Finished goods are output that has completed the production process to a prescribed (saleable) standard and is intended for sale -- this excludes raw materials (an input), semi-finished/in-process goods (not yet complete), and goods made solely for internal use (which would not be 'for sale').

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions para 17
questions.source_excerpt: It excludes intangible assets and assets solely used for post-manufacturing activities such as, sale, storage, distribution, etc.
questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly excluded from ASI's definition of 'Fixed Capital'?
options: Intangible assets, and assets used solely for post-manufacturing activities such as sale, storage, or distribution
Land owned by the factory
Plant and machinery used directly in production
Transport equipment used for moving raw materials within the factory premises
questions.explanation: Fixed Capital is meant to capture productive assets tied to the manufacturing process itself (land, buildings, plant, machinery, transport equipment used in production), so the manual explicitly carves out intangible assets and any assets used purely for downstream activities like sale, storage, or distribution -- these are not part of the factory's productive fixed-asset base as ASI defines it.

questions.locator: Manual on Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Definitions paras 17 and 36
questions.source_excerpt: Fixed Capital represents the depreciated value of fixed assets owned by the factory as on the closing day of the accounting year... [Total Capital] is the total of fixed capital and working capital.
questions.question: 'Fixed Capital' (a stock reported in ASI) and 'capital formation' (a flow used in national accounts) are related but distinct concepts. Which statement correctly captures the distinction?
options: Fixed Capital is a stock -- the depreciated value of assets held at a point in time (the accounting year's close) -- whereas capital formation is a flow, measuring the addition to (or disposal from) that stock of assets during the year
Fixed Capital and capital formation are simply two different names for the exact same quantity, with no conceptual difference
Fixed Capital is measured only in physical units (e.g. number of machines), while capital formation is measured only in monetary units
Capital formation is a stock measured at the start of the year, while Fixed Capital is a flow measured over the year
questions.explanation: This is a standard stock-versus-flow distinction in economic statistics: Fixed Capital, as ASI defines it, is a balance-sheet-style stock valued at a single point in time (the accounting year's close), while capital formation (net or gross) is a flow concept measuring how much new investment was added to (or old capital retired from) that stock over the course of the year -- the two are related (this year's stock roughly equals last year's stock plus net capital formation) but are not interchangeable, and both are expressed in monetary, not physical, units.
